name: Kuman
confidence_why: Bergmann 1966 and Pfantz & Pfantz 2005 both put stress on the first syllable of two- and three-syllable words and differ only over the rare words of four or more syllables, where Bergmann says antepenultimate and Pfantz says "the third syllable", a wording that coincides with Bergmann's at five syllables and is probably a loose rendering of it.

catalog_quote: Ueber die Betonung, dem Druckakzent im Wort, d.h. wenn die Woerter mehr als eine Silbe haben, laesst sich keine bindende Regel aufstellen. Doch gibt es Regeln, die fast ohne Ausnahmen gelten: 1. Dass bei einsilbigen Woertern der Ton auf dieser Silbe liegt ist selbstverstaendlich. 2. Bei zweisilbigen Woertern liegt der Ton fuer gewoehnlich auf der ersten Silbe. Es gibt allerding einige wenige Ausnahmen z.B. porá . 3. Bei dreisilbigen Woertern liegt der Ton normalerweise auf der ersten Silbe. Dabei zaehlt tn und glm im Verb als eigene Silbe(der Nasal ist Silbentraeger). Es gibt sehr wenig Ausnahmen. 4 Bei mehr als dreisilbigen Woertern ist der Ton auf der drittletzten Silbe. Bei sehr langen Woertern kann es neben dem Hauptakzent auch einen oder mehrere Nebenakzente im gleichen Wort geben. [Bergmann 1966:18-19] || In two-and three-syllable words the stress is usually on the first syllable. There are only very few exceptions. In words with four or more syllables the stress is on the third syllable. These long words are fairly uncommon and may all be the result of compounding. Hardie (2003:63-92) identifies a distinction between falling and non-falling tone on Kuman words. However, there are only a few minimal pairs, so tone is not marked in the orthography. There is no contrast between length of vowels or between length of consonants. [Pfantz & Pfantz 2005:22]

new_statements.translation: Concerning stress, the dynamic (pressure) accent in the word, i.e. when words have more than one syllable, no binding rule can be set up. But there are rules that hold almost without exception: 1. That in monosyllabic words the accent lies on that syllable is self-evident. 2. In disyllabic words the accent usually lies on the first syllable. There are, however, a few exceptions, e.g. porá. 3. In trisyllabic words the accent normally lies on the first syllable. [omitted: 'Here tn and glm in the verb count as a syllable of their own (the nasal is syllabic). There are very few exceptions.'] 4. In words of more than three syllables the accent is on the third-from-last syllable. In very long words there may be, besides the main accent, one or more secondary accents in the same word.

Doch gibt es Regeln, die fast ohne Ausnahmen gelten :' then p.19 points 1-4 exactly as quoted (1 monosyllables; 2 disyllables 'fuer gewoehnlich auf der erst…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic word stress falls on the first syllable of di- and trisyllabic words and on the antepenultimate syllable of words of four or more syllables, i.e. an antepenultimate (three-syllable-window, leftmost-when-short) pattern, stated as a strong tendency rather than an exceptionless rule. Immediately after, Bergmann says high/low tone was repeatedly suspected but could not be demonstrated; he attributes the apparent pitch differences to contrastive vowel length (duu 'straight' vs du 'dumb', koro vs kooro), and notes some speakers have marked sentence melody.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Bei sehr langen Woertern kann es neben dem Hauptakzent auch einen oder mehrere Nebenakzente im gleichen Wort geben' -- very long words may carry one or more secondary accents; positions not specified.
new_statements.exceptions: A few disyllables with final stress (e.g. porá); syllabic nasals in verb forms (tn, glm) count as syllables for the count; in the verb chapters (typescript pp.41, 45, 51) negative verb forms stress the negation syllable -kiri- rather than the stem, 1st person dual/plural forms with a long (contracted) u take the accent on that syllable even when it is the penult, and one paradigm is described as stressed on the second syllable owing to vowel fusion ('Das kommt wohl von der Verschmelzung der Vokale, die deshalb gedehnt werden und den Druckakzent bekommen').
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly the word ('Druckakzent im Wort'), citation forms; Bergmann separately remarks that slow/emphatic pronunciation changes the 'Ton' and that sentence melody is pronounced for some speakers. Piau 1985 p.116 independently reports sentence-level prosody: one sentential intonation contour 'with stress occurring penultimately' over a nuclear-juncture clause -- a phrase-level observation, not a word-stress rule. Variety: Kuman of the Ega mission area on the Chimbu river (central Kuman); Kerowagi dialects to the west mentioned only for a consonant difference.
new_statements.identity_note: Bergmann 1966 describes Kuman as spoken around the Lutheran mission at Ega on the Chimbu river (central Kuman, Simbu Province) = Glottolog kuma1280 / iso kue; he mentions Kerowagi-area dialects to the west only for a g~k difference. No sub-variety glottocode applies. Note for PL users: sealang.net's link currently delivers McElhanon (PL-A26.23), not Trefry; use the ANU handle 1885/146470.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog rule (stress on syllable 1 of 2, 1 of 3, 2 of 4, 3 of 5: initial in 2-3-syllable words, antepenult in longer words) for 2-, 3- and 5-syllable words and with the Bergmann 1966 statement of record on those. The only difference is the literal wording for long words: 'on the third syllable' gives 0010 for a 4-syllable word (penult) and 001000 for a 6-syllable word, where the catalog has 0100 and 000100 (antepenult). If 'third syllable' is read as Bergmann's 'drittletzte' (third from the end), which its wording and sourcing make likely, the OPD agrees fully and merely adds that exceptions are very few, that long words are rare compounds, and that a marginal falling/non-fa…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Count-based rule: in words of two or three syllables stress falls on the first syllable (very few exceptions); in words of four or more syllables (rare, probably all compounds) it falls on 'the third syllable'. Taken literally that is the third syllable from the left (penult in a 4-syllable word, antepenult in a 5-syllable word); the four-point structure of the statement mirrors Bergmann 1966's list (monosyllable / disyllable first / trisyllable first / longer words drittletzte = antepenult) and the OPD lists Bergmann's Grammatik in its bibliography, so 'third syllable' is very probably a loose rendering of 'drittletzte', but the text as printed does not say 'third from the end'. The OPD also reports (after Hardie 2003) a falling vs non-falling tone distinction with only a few minimal pairs, unmarked in the orthography, and no vowel- or consonant-length contrast. p.23 adds that the clusters pir~pr, sir~sr, mbir~mbr, tir~tr, dir~dr alternate 'depending on surrounding stress and syllable patterns'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Only very few exceptions' to first-syllable stress in 2-3-syllable words (none listed). Words of 4+ syllables are 'fairly uncommon and may all be the result of compounding'.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Kuman of Simbu Province as a whole (all villages within the boundary it gives along the Wahgi River, the Highlands Highway and the Madang border; population 115,000, 2000 census), with no dialect singled out. Bergmann 1966 describes the variety spoken along the Chimbu River. No work in this item describes another language.

new_statements.relation_note: Same content as the read 2005 entry (tagged held by the project 'read: contradicts the catalog's classification'). Agrees with the catalog/Bergmann 1966 for 1-, 2-, 3- and 5-syllable words (initial, initial, initial, third = antepenult), but for words of four or more syllables it puts stress 'on the third syllable' (counted from the left: penult in a 4-syllable word, 0010), where Bergmann 1966 p.. antepenultimate stress encodes. The difference is confined to rare long words that the OPD itself calls probable compounds; it also adds a marginal tone contrast (Hardie 2003) that Bergmann explicitly doubted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Predictable, non-contrastive stress: word-initial in two- and three-syllable words (very few exceptions); in words of four or more syllables (rare, probably all compounds) stress falls on the third syllable. A marginal falling vs non-falling word-tone distinction (Hardie 2003) with only a few minimal pairs; no length contrast.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (Bergmann 1966 p.19, held, mentions Nebenakzente in very long words; this OPD does not)

tone_statements.citation: 千田俊太郎 [Tida, Syuntarô]. 2010. 近い方言の分岐: シンブー諸語のトーン變化から [The divergence of close dialects: from tonal change in the Simbu languages]. 第28回言語記述研究会, 総合地球環境学研究所 (京都), 2010-05-19 (presentation).
tone_statements.quote: 東シンブー諸語のトーンは音韻的には語を領域とする對立するメロディーである。メロディーのパタンは高 (high)、下降 (falling)、上昇 (rising)、低 (low)、落調 (key-lowering trigger)の五種類にまとめることができる ... キンデコンド語はドム語と同じく語を領域とする三種のメロディーが對立するトーン・システムをもつが、壓倒的多數の語が下降メロディーを持ち、落調トーンが極端に少ない。例へば動詞の活用形は連用形を除き全て下降メロディーをとる。
tone_statements.translation: Phonologically, the tones of the East Simbu languages are contrasting melodies whose domain is the word. The melody patterns can be summed up as five types: high, falling, rising, low and key-lowering trigger ... Kinde Kondo, like Dom, has a tone system in which three word-domain melodies contrast, but the overwhelming majority of words carry the falling melody and the key-lowering tone is extremely rare. For instance, all inflected verb forms except the converb take the falling melody.
tone_statements.locator: sec.2.4 トーン (pp.163-164); inventory also in 表12 'word-tone.. キンデコンド H:F:D' and 表14, sec.3.2 (p.174)
tone_statements.summary: Kinde Kondo (=Kuman): 3 word melodies H, F, D (Table 12 H:F:D). D lowers the key pitch of following words, taken as word-final floating L; author: Hardie 2003's 2-tone analysis may have missed D.

tone_statements.citation: Tida, Syuntarô. 2006. Systems and Correspondences of Simbu Tones: Toward Proto-Tones. Paper presented at the Phonology Association in Kansai (PAIK), Kobe University, 27 January 2006. [= 'Tida 2006b' in Tida 2011: 182.]
tone_statements.quote: キンデコンド語はドム語と同じく語を領域とする三種のメロディーが對立するトーン・システムをもつが、壓倒的多數の語が下降メロディーを持ち、落調トーンが極端に少ない。例へば動詞の活用形は連用形を除き全て下降メロディーをとる。 ... [表 12 クマン諸方言の相違點: バリ・ナウレ / クナナ・ク / キンデコンド] word-tone H:F:R:L H:F:R:L H:F:D ... クマン祖語のトーン對立はキンデコンドでは*F と*R の合流により單純になつたが、それ以外の方言には殘されてゐる。
tone_statements.translation: Kinde Kondo, like Dom, has a tone system in which three melodies with the word as their domain contrast, but the overwhelming majority of words carry the falling melody and the key-lowering tone is extremely rare; e.g. all verb conjugation forms except the converb take the falling melody. ... [Table 12, differences among Kuman dialects: word-tone Bari-Naure H:F:R:L, Kunana Ku H:F:R:L, Kinde Kondo H:F:D] ... The Proto-Kuman tone contrast was simplified in Kinde Kondo by the merger of *F and *R but is retained in the other dialects.
tone_statements.locator: p.164 sec.2.4; Table 12 and following prose p.174 sec.3.2
tone_statements.summary: Word-tone melodies: Kinde Kondo (=Kuman proper, Endugla data) H, F, D (3); Bari-Naure, Kunana Ku H, F, R, L (4). D lowers the next word's key; says Hardie 2003's two-tone analysis may have missed D.

readall_conflicts: One partial disagreement, confined to rare long words. Bergmann 1966 (statement of record, pp.18-19) puts stress on the first syllable of 2- and 3-syllable words and on the 'drittletzte' (antepenultimate) syllable of longer words, i.e. the catalog stress on syllable 1 of 2, 1 of 3, 2 of 4, 3 of 5. The Pfantz OPD (2005, p.22) gives the same first-syllable rule for 2-3-syllable words but says that in 4+-syllable words stress is 'on the third syllable', which read literally is third-from-the-left (0010 for 4 syllables, 001000 for 6) and coincides with the catalog only at 5 syllables. The OPD's four-part wording tracks Bergmann's list and cites his Grammatik, so 'third syllable' is very probably a loose rendering of 'drittletzte'; the OPD itself calls such words 'fairly uncommon' and probably all compounds. The two works also differ on tone: Bergmann (p.19) rejects high/low tone and attributes the impression to vowel length, whereas the OPD reports (from Hardie 2003) a falling vs non-falling tone contrast with few minimal pairs, unwritten, and no length contrast. Neither point changes the placement of stress in ordinary 2-3-syllable words, where all sources agree on the initial syllable. sources.note: pp.18-19 section 'c. Die Betonung': no binding rule but near-exceptionless tendencies: 2- and 3-syllable words stressed on the first syllable (few exceptions, e.g. porá), words of 4+ syllables on the antepenult; very long words may carry secondary accents; tone was suspected but he concludes the contrasts are vowel length, not pitch. Verb chapters (pp.41, 45, 51 of typescript) add morphological detail: verb forms mostly initial/antepenult-stressed, negative forms stress the negation syllable -kiri-, contracted long vowels attract the accent.

tone.quote: 東シンブー諸語のトーンは音韻的には語を領域とする對立するメロディーである。メロディーのパタンは高 (high)、下降 (falling)、上昇 (rising)、低 (low)、落調 (key-lowering trigger)の五種類にまとめることができる ... キンデコンド語はドム語と同じく語を領域とする三種のメロディーが對立するトーン・システムをもつが、壓倒的多數の語が下降メロディーを持ち、落調トーンが極端に少ない。例へば動詞の活用形は連用形を除き全て下降メロディーをとる。
tone.locator: sec.2.4 トーン (pp.163-164); inventory also in 表12 'word-tone.. キンデコンド H:F:D' and 表14, sec.3.2 (p.174)
tone.translation: Phonologically, the tones of the East Simbu languages are contrasting melodies whose domain is the word. The melody patterns can be summed up as five types: high, falling, rising, low and key-lowering trigger ... Kinde Kondo, like Dom, has a tone system in which three word-domain melodies contrast, but the overwhelming majority of words carry the falling melody and the key-lowering tone is extremely rare. For instance, all inflected verb forms except the converb take the falling melody.
